I figured I would write a bit of a story today, a bit about how I decided to come out of the closet as genderfluid.

I realized long ago that something was 'up' with me. A 'one of these things is not like the others' of our family. I was a middle child, amongst 5 kids. The middle boy, second-to-last born. Neither the spoiled first nor the last... the perpetually forgotten one.

From my early adolescence, I was fascinated by women's clothing. My sisters had it, my mom had it, and I wanted to wear it.

But only sometimes. Why only sometimes?

I got caught once. I was trying on my mom's bra, and left it out and stuffed with socks. I was questioned, chuckled at for 'experimenting', and left to my own devices. I was caught playing with makeup once as well, younger. That was likely chalked up to curiosity. My sisters play-fought to put makeup on me once, when I was about 8. I fought at the time, but secretly hoped they succeeded. It was a plastic lipstick tube anyway. I was disappointed.

Eventually, the box was created. Or first, the bag. A backpack stuffed full of panties, a bra, a black woman's shirt, a skirt, and clip-on earrings, and a few other accessories or articles of clothing, all bought with cash or scavenged from 'free' bins in the lobby. A young, adult male, terrifiedly hiding a bag of women's clothing in the closet, pulling it out on the rare occasions my brother, sharing the apartment we'd moved to the city in, would be out of town. He got a girlfriend eventually, who soon also lived in there. My occasions to feel feminine dropped to maybe a few blessed hours once every few months.

I got married in my late 20's. She never knew. Nobody did. I had grown from the 78 pound weakling (that the 98 pound weakling picked on to feel better about themselves) into a tall, lanky male. My brother was short, his girlfriend was short, and that corner of the closet was a bitch to reach even for me. I was careful. My wife is a bit taller, but still had no chance of reaching my hidden box of femininity. Opportunities to access it dropped to once or twice a year. My femininity, forcibly held back by my diligent mannerism-monitoring, begged my brain to be allowed to express herself.

The years passed. As the desire to be feminine grew, so to did my meagre clothing supply. With the internet and a having packages delivered to my work, my personal tastes slowly found themselves. The occasional Forever 21 or similar package came to work, I could chalk it up to being for my wife, who people were told was unable to receive packages at her work. The bag turned into a more refined box, with selected makeup shades and fitting clothes, though pared down to a single outfit to hide better. Once, or twice a year, I would be able to pull it out.

I got to sleep in a bra once, so I could wake up feeling like a girl. It felt wonderful. That was a rare blessing, and may have helped solidify my resolve.

I eventually realized that the vast bulk of people wouldn't care one way or the other what I look like, or how I act, as long as I don't distract them from their own little worlds. Only those paying attention to me would question it.

How could I answer? For my entire life, this was the question I was unable to answer. "Why?"

If you have no acceptable response to a question, the answer will be filled in with the easiest, fastest possible answer by the questioner (broad-sweeping generalization).

Picture this. You open a door, and see a terrified, bearded, middle-aged man wearing makeup and women's clothing, is in front of you. You have never seen this behaviour from this person before in your life. He looks horribly ashamed, and is trying to find a way to not be seen. What do you do?

So I fought my entire life to keep from having to encounter that situation. The box collected dust most of the year.

Then, 'it' happened. Long story short, I got wasted, blacked out, and started blabbing to my wife. That was about 1 year ago, last fall.

It has been an unusual year, due to a whole pile of changes. Layoffs, new careers, more layoffs, clothing, makeup, pierced ears, manicures, and 'the emptying of the box'. Most of that has moved to the drawers in my bedroom, where I now unabashedly put on my bra in the morning beside my wife :)

The ultimate catalyst? Knowledge. You have be capable of answering questions, even if nobody asks them. That way, you won't fear the question.

When I blabbed to my wife, I vaguely remember uttering something about 'lesbian', which from what she tells me, I was trying to ask if she was one. I believe what I was attempting was to say that I was one (which, being a gynesexual genderfluid, is sorta right some of the time). A lesbian in a man's body.

But only sometimes. Why?

Knowledge and research are wonderful things, and with access to for all intents and purposes the entirety of all human knowledge at my fingertips, I just needed to be told what to research.

Someone threw me the word 'cisgender' by blind chance. The googling began. Genderfluid followed shortly thereafter.

Pieces started fitting together. The lifelong puzzle was finally being answered. "Why only sometimes? What's up with this in general?". Genderfluid answered everything. The more I researched, the more other gender terms I crossed off as not fitting, the more I thought about my childhood, and the more everything fell into place.

It all made sense, finally. One simple word would have saved me decades of fear and pain.

It was rough between my wife and I for a while. This was very unexpected, and very unusual. Out of the blue, as it were. Things slowly progressed. Fights were fought, agreements were reached, and slowly, talking began. Last week, I bought my first purse, and we got a mani/pedi together :)

I was lucky on the family front... in a morbid sort of way. Despite growing up way out in Flatlands, Religionville, my siblings have been supportive. Unfortunately long-distance, but supportive :). I no longer have any parents or grandparents remaining, so that saved me from having to deal with that. It's unfortunately made other things more difficult, but one works with what one's got.

...That ended on a bit of a downer :(

Which it really shouldn't, since it makes this sound terrible. Shit happens, and all you can do is power through it. That's one thing that this 78-pound weakling learned over the years... you do whatcha gotta with the situation presented to you. At this point I've done just about everything from office work to heavy construction. I've studies subjects from quantum physics to gender identity. For every job I've worked, I've researched and learned as much as I can. All this knowledge may not seem helpful at the time, but it will be.

The human brain is amazing. You fill it with a variety of subjects and skills, and over time it will take these seemingly disparate pieces of information, and combine them to answer questions you face in life.

That's how I eventually faced my fears. Learning how to answer all of my own questions.

If someone doesn't believe me.... pfft, whatever. I answered it for myself, it's not my job to convince others that genderfluid is a thing. They don't wanna accept my explanation, oh well, they can do their own research then :P

Will those who know me think differently of me? Probably... but once I've learned enough to satisfy myself, my concern about how others think of me seems to disappear.
